techniques.label: Named the feeling
techniques.shortTip: Name what your child feels before you guide.
techniques.why: When a child hears their feeling named, they feel understood, settle faster, and become able to listen.
techniques.goodExample: You're really mad that playtime is over.
patterns: \b(you|you're|youre|you are|you seem|you look|you feel|sounds like you|looks like you|i can see you)\b[^.!?]{0,30}\b(mad|angry|upset|sad|frustrated|disappointed|scared|worried|tired|annoyed|grumpy|jealous|nervous|overwhelmed|hurt)\b
\b(that|this) (is|was|feels) (so |really )?(hard|frustrating|annoying|disappointing|unfair|scary)\b
\byou (really|so) (want|wanted|wish)\b

techniques.label: Connected first
techniques.why: Calm closeness tells a child's alarm system they are safe, which makes cooperation possible.
techniques.goodExample: I'm right here. Come sit with me for a second.
patterns: \b(i'm|i am) (right )?(here|with you|not going anywhere)\b
\b(come here|come sit|let's (hug|cuddle|take a breath|breathe)|can i (hug|hold) you|i love you|you're safe|we'll figure it out|i've got you)\b

techniques.label: Offered a choice
techniques.shortTip: Give two choices you're happy with.
techniques.why: A limited choice gives a child some control, so they don't have to fight for it.
techniques.goodExample: Do you want the blue toothbrush or the green one?

source.name: CDC — Essentials for Parenting Toddlers and Preschoolers

patterns: \b(do you want|would you like|you can choose|you can pick|which one|which do you|you get to choose|you get to pick|want to)\b[^?]{0,60}\bor\b
\b\w+ or (?!else\b)\w+( one)?\s*\?

techniques.label: Made it playful
techniques.shortTip: Turn the task into a game.
techniques.why: Play lowers stress and invites cooperation without a power struggle.
techniques.goodExample: Can your toothbrush find all the sugar bugs hiding in there?

source.name: PCIT International — PRIDE skills (Parent-Child Interaction Therapy)

patterns: \b(let's pretend|pretend|i bet you can't|race you|let's race|can you (roar|hop|jump|stomp|be a)|silly|monster|sugar bugs|magic|tickle)\b
\blike a (lion|rocket|robot|dinosaur|bunny|frog|superhero|race car)\b

techniques.label: Used when–then
techniques.shortTip: Link the task to what comes next.
techniques.why: A when–then sentence makes the routine predictable instead of a battle of wills.
techniques.goodExample: When your teeth are clean, then we'll read your story.

source.name: CDC — Essentials for Parenting Toddlers and Preschoolers

patterns: \b(when|as soon as|once)\b[^.!?]{1,60}\b(then|we can|we'll|you can|you get to)\b
\bfirst\b[^.!?]{1,60}\bthen\b

techniques.label: Set a calm limit
techniques.shortTip: Hold the limit calmly, without threats.
techniques.why: A calm, clear limit shows the child you're in charge and on their side at the same time.
techniques.goodExample: I won't let you throw the toothbrush. I'll keep it safe until you're ready.

source.name: AAP Policy Statement: Effective Discipline to Raise Healthy Children (Pediatrics, 2018)

patterns: \b(i won't let you|i'm not going to let you|i will not let you|it's not okay to|it is not okay to|i can't let you|the rule is|we don't (hit|throw|kick|bite))\b
\b(it's|it is) (time|bedtime) (to|for)\b

techniques.label: Praised the effort
techniques.shortTip: Praise exactly what they did right.
techniques.why: Specific praise tells the child which behavior to repeat and builds connection.
techniques.goodExample: Thank you for opening your mouth so wide!

source.name: PCIT International — PRIDE skills (Parent-Child Interaction Therapy)

patterns: \b(thank you for|thanks for|great job|good job|nice job|way to go|i love (how|that) you|i'm proud of (you|how)|you did it)\b

techniques.label: Threat
techniques.shortTip: Swap the threat for a choice or a when–then.
techniques.why: Threats set off a child's alarm system: they dig in harder or comply out of fear, and trust takes a hit.

source.name: AAP Policy Statement: Effective Discipline to Raise Healthy Children (Pediatrics, 2018)

patterns: \b(or else|if you don't|if you do not|you're going to lose|you will lose|i'll take (it|your|away)|i will take|you won't get|you're not getting|you are not getting|straight to bed|time-?out|go to your room|i'm (going to|gonna) (take|leave|call))\b
\bno (ipad|tablet|tv|screens?|story|stories|dessert|toys?|games?|park|playdate|treats?)\b

techniques.label: Yelling or name-calling
techniques.shortTip: Lower your voice; describe the behavior, not the child.
techniques.why: Harsh words and yelling raise fear and shame, which makes meltdowns longer and more frequent.

source.name: AAP Policy Statement: Effective Discipline to Raise Healthy Children (Pediatrics, 2018)

patterns: \b(stop being (a|such a) (baby|brat)|you're (being )?(a |such a )?(baby|brat|bad|naughty|annoying|ridiculous|impossible|spoiled)|shut up|stupid|what is wrong with you|you're driving me crazy)\b

techniques.label: Lecture
techniques.shortTip: Keep it to one short sentence while they're upset.
techniques.why: An upset child can't take in long explanations; save the lesson for a calm moment.
patterns: \b(how many times|you need to understand|when i was your age|do you know how (much|hard)|you always|you never|we've talked about this|i've told you)\b

techniques.label: Dismissed the feeling
techniques.shortTip: Accept the feeling, then guide the behavior.
techniques.why: When a feeling is brushed off, the child usually has to show it louder to be heard.
patterns: \b(stop crying|stop whining|it's not a big deal|it's no big deal|you're fine|you are fine|calm down|don't be (sad|mad|upset|silly|a baby)|there's nothing to (cry|be upset) about|get over it|that's enough crying|big kids don't cry)\b

techniques.label: Asked 'why'
techniques.shortTip: Guess the feeling instead of asking why.
techniques.why: Upset young kids can't explain why; the question feels like blame and adds pressure.
patterns: \bwhy (are|do|would|did|can't|won't|is it|must) you\b

techniques.label: Bribe
techniques.shortTip: Use when–then for routines instead of rewards for stopping.
techniques.why: Rewarding a child for stopping a meltdown can teach that meltdowns pay off.
patterns: \b(i'll give you|i'll buy you|i'll get you|you can have (a |some )?(candy|treat|cookie|ice cream|sweets|chocolate|lollipop|toy)|if you stop (crying|screaming|whining)[^.!?]{0,40}(candy|treat|cookie|ice cream|toy|chocolate|screen|ipad|tablet))\b
